techniques.name: Conformal Prediction
techniques.description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

example_use_cases.description: A medicinal chemistry team screening compounds in silico builds prediction sets of the protein targets each compound may be active against, at 95% coverage. Compounds with a single-target set go to lab testing for that target, and those with several targets go to a wider panel, so costly experiments follow how uncertain the model is.

Providing transparent multi-class predictions in judicial risk assessment by showing all plausible risk categories at the stated coverage level, enabling judges to see the full range of possibilities rather than just a single point estimate.

A university predicts whether first-year students will complete their degree and offers early support when the 90% prediction set includes 'withdraws'. To keep that 90% true for every group, not only on average, the data team calibrates the sets separately within each demographic group, then checks coverage and average set size per group on held-out students. A group with too few calibration cases is reported as not covered by the guarantee.

limitations.description: Sets can be wide enough to be useless. A multi-class set holding most classes, or an interval spanning the plausible range, meets the coverage target but tells the decision-maker little, and sets containing opposing outcomes make decisions hard. Width depends on the model's quality and the scoring rule chosen, and the guarantee says nothing about it.

Needs labelled calibration data kept apart from training. On small datasets that means less data to train on, or a coarse and unstable coverage level, and variants that avoid a separate calibration set need several model fits.

The guarantee assumes calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. Drift, a changed population or strongly time-ordered data break it, and coverage then falls below target with no warning. In Shafer and Vovk's example, a nominal 5% error rate rose to 8% on a systematically different test set.

Coverage is guaranteed on average over all cases, not for each individual or subgroup, so a model can reach 95% overall while covering a minority group far less often. Mondrian calibration fixes this only for predefined, non-overlapping groups. It needs each new case's group at prediction time and is unstable when a group has few calibration cases (MAPIE's tutorial gives under 200 as an example).

Cost depends on the variant. Split conformal prediction adds little beyond scoring a held-out set, but full conformal prediction re-evaluates every candidate outcome and cross-conformal variants refit the model several times, which can be prohibitive for large models or real-time use.

resources.title: A tutorial on conformal prediction
resources.abstract: Conformal prediction uses past experience to determine precise levels of confidence in new predictions. Given an error probability $ε$, together with a method that makes a prediction $\hat{y}$ of a label $y$, it produces a set of labels, typically containing $\hat{y}$, that also contains $y$ with probability $1-ε$. Conformal prediction can be applied to any method for producing $\hat{y}$: a nearest-neighbor method, a support-vector machine, ridge regression, etc.   Conformal prediction is designed for an on-line setting in which labels are predicted successively, each one being revealed before the next is predicted. The most novel and valuable feature of conformal prediction is that if the successive examples are sampled independently from the same distribution, then the successive predictions will be right $1-ε$ of the time, even though they are based on an accumulating dataset rather than on independent datasets.   In addition to the model under which successive examples are sampled independently, other on-line compression models can also use conformal prediction. The widely used Gaussian linear model is one of these.   This tutorial presents a self-contained account of the theory of conformal prediction and works through several numerical examples. A more comprehensive treatment of the topic is provided in "Algorithmic Learning in a Random World", by Vladimir Vovk, Alex Gammerman, and Glenn Shafer (Springer, 2005).

resources.title: Estimating diagnostic uncertainty in artificial intelligence assisted pathology using conformal prediction
resources.abstract: Unreliable predictions can occur when an artificial intelligence (AI) system is presented with data it has not been exposed to during training. We demonstrate the use of conformal prediction to detect unreliable predictions, using histopathological diagnosis and grading of prostate biopsies as example. We digitized 7788 prostate biopsies from 1192 men in the STHLM3 diagnostic study, used for training, and 3059 biopsies from 676 men used for testing. With conformal prediction, 1 in 794 (0.1%) predictions is incorrect for cancer diagnosis (compared to 14 errors [2%] without conformal prediction) while 175 (22%) of the predictions are flagged as unreliable when the AI-system is presented with new data from the same lab and scanner that it was trained on. Conformal prediction could with small samples ( N = 49 for external scanner, N = 10 for external lab and scanner, and N = 12 for external lab, scanner and pathology assessment) detect systematic differences in external data leading to worse predictive performance. The AI-system with conformal prediction commits 3 (2%) errors for cancer detection in cases of atypical prostate tissue compared to 44 (25%) without conformal prediction, while the system flags 143 (80%) unreliable predictions. We conclude that conformal prediction can increase patient safety of AI-systems.

sample_claims.text: On a held-out test set from the same patient population as the calibration data, the 95% prediction sets contained the true diagnosis in at least 95% of cases, within sampling error.
Prediction-set coverage on the latest quarter of live data stays within the agreed margin of its nominal level, so there is no sign that the exchangeability assumption has broken down in deployment.

For the perception model, the 95% prediction sets contained the true object class in at least 95% of held-out frames, and frames whose set holds more than one class trigger the cautious fallback behaviour.
Every credit-limit recommendation is shown with a set of plausible limit bands at 90% coverage, and any case whose set holds more than one band is routed to a human underwriter.

The 90% prediction sets are calibrated separately within each demographic group, and on held-out cases their coverage is within three percentage points of 90% in every group, with each group's number of calibration and test cases reported.

techniques.name: Platt Scaling
techniques.description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

resources.title: Assessing calibration and bias of a deployed machine learning malnutrition prediction model within a large healthcare system
resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

sample_claims.text: After Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes, the default model's predicted probabilities agree with observed default rates in every score decile, within the tolerance set in the model risk policy.

After Platt scaling, the defect classifier's log loss on the held-out test set is lower than before, and its reliability diagram shows predicted defect rates within the tolerance set in the quality plan.

Each flagged claim is shown to caseworkers with a probability calibrated against held-out review outcomes, and the calibration curve and its meaning are published in the caseworker guidance, so a displayed 30 per cent corresponds to roughly 30 in 100 similar claims needing correction.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

sample_claims.text: On a test set not used to fit the temperature, the diagnostic model's expected calibration error is below the agreed threshold, and observed accuracy in each confidence band is within tolerance of its stated confidence.

Calibrating the credit risk model with a single temperature left its predicted classes, and therefore its accuracy, unchanged, while its default probabilities now track the observed default rates on held-out data.
A displayed confidence of 80% corresponds to about 80 correct predictions in 100, as shown by a reliability diagram on data not used to fit the temperature.
After refitting the temperature on a labelled sample from the new region, the land-cover classifier's calibration error on that region's test data is no worse than on the original region.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.

resources.title: Deep ensembles segmentation tutorial using the MUAD dataset - TorchUncertainty Docs
Uncertainty-aware body composition analysis with deep regression ensembles on UK Biobank MRI
resources.abstract: Along with rich health-related metadata, medical images have been acquired for over 40,000 male and female UK Biobank participants, aged 44-82, since 2014. Phenotypes derived from these images, such as measurements of body composition from MRI, can reveal new links between genetics, cardiovascular disease, and metabolic conditions. In this work, six measurements of body composition and adipose tissues were automatically estimated by image-based, deep regression with ResNet50 neural networks from neck-to-knee body MRI. Despite the potential for high speed and accuracy, these networks produce no output segmentations that could indicate the reliability of individual measurements. The presented experiments therefore examine uncertainty quantification with mean-variance regression and ensembling to estimate individual measurement errors and thereby identify potential outliers, anomalies, and other failure cases automatically. In 10-fold cross-validation on data of about 8500 subjects, mean-variance regression and ensembling showed complementary benefits, reducing the mean absolute error across all predictions by 12%. Both improved the calibration of uncertainties and their ability to identify high prediction errors. With intra-class correlation coefficients (ICC) above 0.97, all targets except the liver fat content yielded relative measurement errors below 5%. Testing on another 1000 subjects showed consistent performance, and the method was finally deployed for inference to 30,000 subjects with missing reference values. The results indicate that deep regression ensembles could ultimately provide automated, uncertainty-aware measurements of body composition for more than 120,000 UK Biobank neck-to-knee body MRI that are to be acquired within the coming years.

sample_claims.text: On held-out scans, the imaging model's ensemble uncertainty is higher for cases it gets wrong than for cases it gets right, so scans above the uncertainty threshold can be sent for manual review.
The ensemble's predicted probabilities are calibrated on held-out data, so that predictions made with 90% confidence are correct about 90% of the time.
When shown inputs from a class absent from the training data, the ensemble's disagreement is measurably higher than on in-distribution inputs, as tested on a held-out set of unseen-class examples.

The driving system reports an uncertainty level with each detection, derived from disagreement between independently trained networks, and remote operators are alerted when it passes the documented limit.
Each credit score shown to underwriters carries an uncertainty range from the ensemble, and scores with a wide range are labelled as low-confidence.

techniques.name: Bootstrap Ensembles
techniques.description: Bootstrap ensembles estimate how much a model's predictions depend on the particular sample of data it was trained on. The training set is resampled with replacement many times, each resample (a bootstrap replicate) holding as many cases as the original so that some cases are repeated and others left out; one model is trained on each replicate with the same settings, and every new input is passed through all of the models. The spread of the models' predictions for an input, reported as a standard deviation or as a range between percentiles, estimates the uncertainty in the model's prediction for that input, and inputs where the models disagree are those the training data constrain least. The spread covers uncertainty in the fitted model only, not the random variation in individual outcomes, so an interval meant to contain a case's actual outcome must add an estimate of that noise, for example from the models' errors on held-out data. Putting a confidence interval around a measured performance score is a different procedure, which resamples the evaluation set and retrains nothing; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics.

example_use_cases.description: An electricity network operator forecasting next-day demand at each substation trains 100 gradient-boosted models on bootstrap replicates of three years of meter readings, resampled in whole-week blocks because consecutive readings are correlated. Planners hold extra reserve at substations where the models' forecasts spread widely, because those are the sites whose forecasts the historical data settle least.

A hospital's readmission-risk tool shows clinicians, beside each patient's predicted risk, the range of risks given by models trained on bootstrap replicates of the training cohort, resampling patients rather than admissions so that one patient's admissions stay together, so that a clinician can see when an estimate rests on few comparable past patients and give it less weight in discharge planning.

A local authority reviewing a housing-need scoring model compares the average spread of bootstrap-ensemble scores across applicant groups and finds it widest for a group with few past applications, which shows that the model's scores for that group are least settled by the data; it collects more cases before letting the scores inform priority for that group.

limitations.description: Every member of the ensemble is a full training run, and every prediction must be made by every member, so training cost, storage and prediction time all grow in proportion to the number of replicates. For large neural networks this usually limits the ensemble to a handful of members, too few for stable percentiles of the spread.

The spread measures uncertainty in the fitted model, not the noise in outcomes. Presented as the range within which a case's actual outcome will fall, it understates the uncertainty, most of all where outcomes are noisy and training data plentiful, so the outcome noise has to be estimated separately, for example from held-out errors, and added.

The spread reflects only what the procedure lets vary: which cases are in each training set and, for models trained from a random start such as neural networks, each member's starting point. Fixed choices such as features, architecture and training settings add no spread. A model consistently wrong for a group the data under-represent can show little spread there, and members can agree closely on inputs unlike the training data, so a small spread is not evidence of reliability.

Each replicate contains on average only about 63 per cent of the distinct training cases, so each member learns from less information than a model trained on all the data. With small datasets or rare classes, some replicates may contain almost none of a rare class or subgroup, which inflates the spread for those cases and can leave individual members unusable.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. With repeated measurements of the same person, time series or other grouped data, case resampling spreads related cases across replicates and understates the uncertainty, unless whole groups or time blocks are resampled instead.

resources.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
resources.abstract: We discuss the following problem: given a random sample X = (X1, X2, …, Xn) from an unknown probability distribution F, estimate the sampling distribution of some prespecified random variable R(X, F), on the basis of the observed data x. (Standard jackknife theory gives an approximate mean and variance in the case R(X, F) = θ(F̂) − θ(F), θ some parameter of interest.) A general method, called the "bootstrap," is introduced, and shown to work satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is shown to be a linear approximation method for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds by a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

resources.title: Practical Confidence and Prediction Intervals
resources.abstract: We  propose  a  new  method to compute prediction intervals.  Espe(cid:173) cially for small data sets the width of a prediction interval does not  only depend on the variance of the target distribution, but also on  the accuracy of our estimator of the mean of the target, i.e., on the  width  of the  confidence  interval.  The  confidence  interval  follows  from the variation in an ensemble of neural networks,  each of them  trained and stopped on bootstrap replicates of the original data set.  A second improvement is the use of the residuals on validation pat(cid:173) terns  instead of on training patterns for  estimation of the variance  of the  target  distribution.  As  illustrated  on  a  synthetic  example,  our method is  better than existing methods with regard to extrap(cid:173) olation and interpolation in data regimes with a limited amount of  data, and yields prediction intervals which  actual confidence  levels  are closer  to the desired  confidence  levels.

sample_claims.text: For each substation's next-day demand forecast, the spread across models trained on bootstrap replicates of the historical data, resampled in whole-week blocks, is reported, and forecasts whose spread exceeds the planning tolerance are flagged.
The flood model's uncertainty for each river gauge reflects how much its predictions change when it is retrained on versions of the gauge records resampled in blocks of consecutive days.
Each readmission-risk score shown to clinicians is accompanied by the range of scores produced by models trained on resampled versions of the training cohort.
The spread of the housing-need model's scores across bootstrap-trained models has been compared between applicant groups and is reported for each group.

techniques.name: Jackknife Resampling
techniques.description: Jackknife resampling, also called leave-one-out resampling, shows how much a result computed from a dataset depends on any single record. The result can be a model's coefficients, its predictions or a performance score; it is recomputed n times on a dataset of n records, leaving out a different record each time and refitting the model where the result depends on one. The spread of the recomputed results, after a standard rescaling, estimates the bias and variance of the original result, meaning how far it would move with a slightly different sample. Records whose removal moves the result most are flagged as influential, and may be outliers or data errors worth checking. The method assumes the records are independent and that no single record changes the result abruptly.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital data team fits a readmission-risk model on 600 patient records and refits it 600 times, leaving out one patient each time. The spread of the refitted coefficients shows which risk factors are stable enough to report, and the records whose removal shifts the fit most go back to clinicians to check for entry errors.

A water utility's analysts estimate how rainfall drives reservoir inflow from 40 annual observations. Leaving out each year in turn gives a variance estimate for the fitted slope and shows whether a single flood year drives the result, before the figure goes into a planning document.

A credit-risk team documents its scorecard's stability for model validators by refitting it with each of 800 sampled loan records left out. It reports the records whose removal changes any coefficient by more than a stated tolerance, so validators can see how much of the model rests on a few loans.

limitations.description: Computationally heavy when the result needs a model refit, since n records mean n refits, which is impractical for datasets with thousands or millions of records or for costly training. Simple statistics that are cheap to recompute do not have this problem.

Works only for statistics that change smoothly when one record is removed. For quantities that jump, such as the number of clusters in a mixture model, leave-one-out estimates are unreliable. Even for smooth statistics the variance estimate tends to run high, so intervals are conservative.

Assumes the records are independent. With repeated or clustered measurements, such as several visits per patient or neighbouring regions, leaving out one record leaves its close relatives in the data, so the refits barely change and the spread understates the true uncertainty.
Provides limited insight into model behaviour on truly novel data, as each jackknife sample is only minimally different from the full training set.

Measures how sensitive a result is to the sample in hand, not whether the model is right. A stable fit can still be systematically wrong, so a narrow spread across refits is no evidence of accuracy, or of performance on a different population.

resources.title: Notes on bias in estimation
resources.abstract: 1. One of the commonest problems in statistics is, given a series of observations Xj, xit..., xn, to find a function of these, tn(xltxit..., xn), which should provide an estimate of an unknown parameter 0. The desirable properties of estimation procedures have been discussed fully elsewhere. They are: (a) That the estimator should be efficient according to some definition of efficiency pre-viously arranged. Most commonly, the reciprocal of the variance of the estimates is taken as a measure of its efficiency, as this is most useful where central limit theory may be relevant. techniques.name: Confidence Thresholding
techniques.description: Confidence thresholding uses a model score to decide whether a prediction should proceed automatically or receive different handling. For classification, a defined reject variant accepts the most likely class only when its estimated probability exceeds a chosen threshold and otherwise withholds the automatic decision. Thresholds can route withheld cases to specified review or fallback procedures, but those procedures require their own validation. Recording the score, threshold and resulting route makes the decision rule inspectable. The operating point trades automatic coverage against accepted errors, and an estimated score is not a guarantee that a decision is correct or safe.

example_use_cases.description: Implementing tiered confidence thresholds in autonomous vehicle decision-making where high-confidence lane changes (>98%) execute automatically, medium-confidence decisions (85-98%) trigger additional sensor verification, and low-confidence situations (<85%) engage conservative defensive driving modes or request human takeover.

A diabetic eye-screening service has its image classifier pass the cases it is least sure about to an ophthalmologist. The service picks the referral share, for example the least certain 10 to 20 per cent of images, so that accuracy on the cases handled automatically meets its target.

A payment processor's fraud model approves transactions it scores as clearly legitimate, runs extra automated checks on middling scores, and sends the least certain ones to an analyst. The thresholds are set so that the analyst queue stays within the team's daily capacity.

A council's tool that flags possible errors in benefit claims shows caseworkers whether each flag is above or below its confidence threshold. The council publishes the share of claims sent to manual review and the error rate among those handled automatically, so the public can see when the tool declines to decide.

limitations.description: Many models produce poorly calibrated confidence scores that don't accurately reflect true prediction uncertainty, leading to overconfident predictions for incorrect outputs or underconfident scores for correct predictions.

Threshold selection requires careful calibration and domain expertise, as inappropriate thresholds can either overwhelm human reviewers with too many cases or miss genuinely uncertain decisions that need oversight.

High-confidence predictions may still be incorrect or harmful, particularly when models encounter adversarial inputs, out-of-distribution data, or systematic biases that the confidence mechanism doesn't detect.
Static thresholds may become inappropriate over time as model performance degrades, data distribution shifts occur, or operational contexts change, requiring ongoing monitoring and adjustment.
Withholding a prediction does not make the subsequent process safe. Review delays, failed routing and inadequate fallback capacity can undermine the intended safeguard.

Leveraging uncertainty information from deep neural networks for disease detection
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) has revolutionized the field of computer vision and image processing. In medical imaging, algorithmic solutions based on DL have been shown to achieve high performance on tasks that previously required medical experts. However, DL-based solutions for disease detection have been proposed without methods to quantify and control their uncertainty in a decision. In contrast, a physician knows whether she is uncertain about a case and will consult more experienced colleagues if needed. Here we evaluate drop-out based Bayesian uncertainty measures for DL in diagnosing diabetic retinopathy (DR) from fundus images and show that it captures uncertainty better than straightforward alternatives. Furthermore, we show that uncertainty informed decision referral can improve diagnostic performance. Experiments across different networks, tasks and datasets show robust generalization. Depending on network capacity and task/dataset difficulty, we surpass 85% sensitivity and 80% specificity as recommended by the NHS when referring 0−20% of the most uncertain decisions for further inspection. We analyse causes of uncertainty by relating intuitions from 2D visualizations to the high-dimensional image space. While uncertainty is sensitive to clinically relevant cases, sensitivity to unfamiliar data samples is task dependent, but can be rendered more robust.

sample_claims.text: The vehicle's planner switches to its conservative fallback whenever perception confidence falls below the validated threshold.
Screening results the model is least certain about are referred to a clinician, and the error rate among results released without review stays within the clinical target at the chosen threshold.
Transactions scoring below the review threshold go to an analyst, and the resulting review queue stays within the fraud team's agreed daily capacity.
The deferral rate and the error rate among automatically handled cases at the operating threshold are documented and reported to the oversight board.
Each prediction shown to staff carries its confidence level, and predictions below the threshold are labelled as low confidence.

techniques.name: Knowledge Boundary Probing
techniques.description: Knowledge boundary probing maps what a language model can and cannot reliably answer. A probe set is built from questions across the topics the system will face, including some with known answers and some that cannot be answered. Each question is asked in several phrasings, because a model may answer one wording correctly and fail on another. Responses are scored for correctness, for whether the model signals doubt when it should, and for whether its stated or computed confidence tracks whether it is right. The result is a topic-by-topic map of what the model knows, knows only under some phrasings, and does not know, which informs where to deploy it, what to tell users about its limits, and where to add training data or human review.

example_use_cases.description: A government analytics team using an LLM to summarise policy evidence probes it on well-researched areas and on recent or local policy it cannot have seen in training. Accuracy drops on the second group, so the team adds a retrieval step for those topics before the tool is used in briefings.

A bank adds a per-topic table of probe results (accurate on card fees, weak on mortgage rules) to the model documentation for its customer-service chatbot. The app uses the table to tell customers when to check with an adviser.

A school-software vendor checks an LLM maths tutor against each curriculum unit, asking every question in several wordings. Units where correctness changes with the wording are marked for teacher review instead of being shown to students unsupervised.

limitations.description: The probe set samples a finite number of topics and question types. A clean result on those says little about topics the set omits, so the map is only as broad as the probes, and mapping every domain is infeasible.

Whether a model 'knows' something depends on how the question is worded. A single phrasing can understate or overstate what the model knows, so each question needs several phrasings, and the boundary is fuzzy rather than a clean line.

Models can be confidently wrong, and can hedge on things they know, so stated or computed confidence is only a rough guide to knowledge. Calibration also varies by topic, so one overall score can hide weak areas.

Scoring needs labelled questions and a way to detect hedging. Deciding which questions are truly unanswerable takes human judgement, and detectors built on one model's uncertainty phrases may miss how other models express doubt.
The map holds for one model version. Fine-tuning, a model update or added retrieval shifts the boundary, so the probes must be rerun after each change to keep the map accurate.

resources.title: Benchmarking Knowledge Boundary for Large Language Models: A Different Perspective on Model Evaluation
resources.abstract: In recent years, substantial advancements have been made in the development of large language models, achieving remarkable performance across diverse tasks. To evaluate the knowledge ability of language models, previous studies have proposed lots of benchmarks based on question-answering pairs. We argue that it is not reliable and comprehensive to evaluate language models with a fixed question or limited paraphrases as the query, since language models are sensitive to prompt. Therefore, we introduce a novel concept named knowledge boundary to encompass both prompt-agnostic and prompt-sensitive knowledge within language models. Knowledge boundary avoids prompt sensitivity in language model evaluations, rendering them more dependable and robust. To explore the knowledge boundary for a given model, we propose projected gradient descent method with semantic constraints, a new algorithm designed to identify the optimal prompt for each piece of knowledge. Experiments demonstrate a superior performance of our algorithm in computing the knowledge boundary compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we evaluate the ability of multiple language models in several domains with knowledge boundary.

resources.title: Do Large Language Models Know What They Don’t Know?
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have a wealth of knowledge that allows them to excel in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks.Current research focuses on enhancing their performance within their existing knowledge.Despite their vast knowledge, LLMs are still limited by the amount of information they can accommodate and comprehend.Therefore, the ability to understand their own limitations on the unknows, referred to as self-knowledge, is of paramount importance.This study aims to evaluate LLMs' self-knowledge by assessing their ability to identify unanswerable or unknowable questions.We introduce an automated methodology to detect uncertainty in the responses of these models, providing a novel measure of their self-knowledge.We further introduce a unique dataset, SelfAware, consisting of unanswerable questions from five diverse categories and their answerable counterparts.Our extensive analysis, involving 20 LLMs including GPT-3, InstructGPT, and LLaMA, discovering an intrinsic capacity for self-knowledge within these models.Moreover, we demonstrate that in-context learning and instruction tuning can further enhance this self-knowledge.Despite this promising insight, our findings also highlight a considerable gap between the capabilities of these models and human proficiency in recognizing the limits of their knowledge. "True wisdom is knowing what you don't know." -Confucius

resources.title: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods
resources.abstract: The notion of uncertainty is of major importance in machine learning and constitutes a key element of machine learning methodology. In line with the statistical tradition, uncertainty has long been perceived as almost synonymous with standard probability and probabilistic predictions. Yet, due to the steadily increasing relevance of machine learning for practical applications and related issues such as safety requirements, new problems and challenges have recently been identified by machine learning scholars, and these problems may call for new methodological developments. In particular, this includes the importance of distinguishing between (at least) two different types of uncertainty, often referred to as aleatoric and epistemic . In this paper, we provide an introduction to the topic of uncertainty in machine learning as well as an overview of attempts so far at handling uncertainty in general and formalizing this distinction in particular.

resources.title: Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

techniques.name: Out-of-Domain Detection
techniques.description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Scope is defined by examples, such as an assistant's supported intents (the actions it can recognise), and a detector then scores how closely each new query resembles them. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. A query judged out of scope can be declined, handed to a person or another service, or answered with a request to rephrase, instead of receiving an unreliable or invented answer. The detector tests resemblance to the defined scope, not what the system actually knows, so it needs evaluating on realistic out-of-scope queries.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a medical chatbot specialised in diabetes management to recognise and deflect questions about unrelated conditions, avoiding potentially dangerous medical advice outside its training domain.

Ensuring an educational AI tutor for high school mathematics reliably identifies advanced university-level questions and redirects students to appropriate resources rather than attempting explanations beyond its scope.

An insurer's claims-intake assistant is built for routine motor and household claims. Messages about unfamiliar claim types, such as large flood events or commercial losses, are detected and routed to a specialist adjuster instead of being handled with irrelevant questions.

A council's resident-services chatbot covers bin collections, parking permits and council tax. When a resident asks about something it does not cover, such as a planning dispute, it says so, names the service that can help and logs the query, and the log shows the council which topics residents ask about that the chatbot cannot answer.

limitations.description: Scope has to be defined before it can be detected, and general-purpose assistants or fuzzy domains have no clean edge. A narrow definition refuses legitimate queries, and a loose one lets unsupported queries through.

Detection is weakest on queries that resemble in-scope ones. In the 2019 benchmark that introduced the task, no intent classifier caught more than about two-thirds of out-of-scope queries even when trained on examples of them, so recall should be measured on realistic out-of-scope queries before the detector is relied on.
The threshold trades wrongly refusing valid queries against wrongly answering unsupported ones. The two errors rarely cost the same, and queries near the boundary will still land on both sides.
Users can rephrase or disguise an unsupported request so that it resembles in-scope wording. A detector tested only on plain phrasings overstates how well it holds up against paraphrase.

Scope changes as capabilities are added or retired, so the detector and its out-of-scope test set need refreshing, or it will refuse newly supported queries and accept newly unsupported ones. Building realistic out-of-scope examples is costly because annotators need expert knowledge of the in-scope intents.

resources.title: An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction
resources.abstract: Task-oriented dialog systems need to know when a query falls outside their range of supported intents, but current text classification corpora only define label sets that cover every example. We introduce a new dataset that includes queries that are out-of-scope—i.e., queries that do not fall into any of the system’s supported intents. This poses a new challenge because models cannot assume that every query at inference time belongs to a system-supported intent class. Our dataset also covers 150 intent classes over 10 domains, capturing the breadth that a production task-oriented agent must handle. We evaluate a range of benchmark classifiers on our dataset along with several different out-of-scope identification schemes. We find that while the classifiers perform well on in-scope intent classification, they struggle to identify out-of-scope queries. Our dataset and evaluation fill an important gap in the field, offering a way of more rigorously and realistically benchmarking text classification in task-driven dialog systems.

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio and checked on a later year of policies, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction matches the observed claim rate and no price band systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set. Because each step matches the observed rate exactly on the cases it was fitted to, calibration checked on those same cases looks perfect whatever its true quality, so it must be checked on separate cases. The two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better on small sets; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.

resources.title: Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates
resources.abstract: Class membership probability estimates are important for many applications of data mining in which classification outputs are combined with other sources of information for decision-making, such as example-dependent misclassification costs, the outputs of other classifiers, or domain knowledge. Previous calibration methods apply only to two-class problems. Here, we show how to obtain accurate probability estimates for multiclass problems by combining calibrated binary probability estimates. We also propose a new method for obtaining calibrated two-class probability estimates that can be applied to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples. Using naive Bayes and support vector machine classifiers, we give experimental results from a variety of two-class and multiclass domains, including direct marketing, text categorization and digit recognition.

resources.title: Predicting suicide attempts in adolescents with longitudinal clinical data and machine learning
resources.abstract: Background Adolescents have high rates of nonfatal suicide attempts, but clinically practical risk prediction remains a challenge. Screening can be time consuming to implement at scale, if it is done at all. Computational algorithms may predict suicide risk using only routinely collected clinical data. We used a machine learning approach validated on longitudinal clinical data in adults to address this challenge in adolescents. Methods This is a retrospective, longitudinal cohort study. Data were collected from the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative from January 1998 to December 2015 and included 974 adolescents with nonfatal suicide attempts and multiple control comparisons: 496 adolescents with other self‐injury ( OSI ), 7,059 adolescents with depressive symptoms, and 25,081 adolescent general hospital controls. Candidate predictors included diagnostic, demographic, medication, and socioeconomic factors. Outcome was determined by multiexpert review of electronic health records. Random forests were validated with optimism adjustment at multiple time points (from 1 week to 2 years). Recalibration was done via isotonic regression. Evaluation metrics included discrimination ( AUC , sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall) and calibration (calibration plots, slope/intercept, Brier score). Results Computational models performed well and did not require face‐to‐face screening. Performance improved as suicide attempts became more imminent. Discrimination was good in comparison with OSI controls ( AUC = 0.83 [0.82–0.84] at 720 days; AUC = 0.85 [0.84–0.87] at 7 days) and depressed controls ( AUC = 0.87 [95% CI 0.85–0.90] at 720 days; 0.90 [0.85–0.94] at 7 days) and best in comparison with general hospital controls ( AUC 0.94 [0.92–0.96] at 720 days; 0.97 [0.95–0.98] at 7 days). Random forests significantly outperformed logistic regression in every comparison. Recalibration improved performance as much as ninefold – clinical recommendations with poorly calibrated predictions can lead to decision errors. Conclusions Machine learning on longitudinal clinical data may provide a scalable approach to broaden screening for risk of nonfatal suicide attempts in adolescents.
